questions.q: To where did Hezekiah send messengers and to whom did he write letters?
questions.a: Hezekiah sent messengers to all of Israel and Judah, and wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh.

questions.q: What did Hezekiah’s message tell them?
questions.a: The message told them they should come to Jerusalem to the house of Yahweh to celebrate the Passover.

questions.q: Who were they that consulted together, to celebrate the Passover in the second month?
questions.a: They were the king, his leaders, and all the assembly in Jerusalem.

questions.q: Why could they not celebrate the Passover right away?
questions.a: They could not celebrate the Passover right away, because there were not sufficient numbers of consecrated priests, nor had the people gathered in Jerusalem.

questions.q: How did this plan appear to the king and all the assembly?
questions.a: The plan appeared to be right in their eyes.

questions.q: What did the king and all the assembly establish and make?
questions.a: They established a decree and made a proclamation.

questions.q: To where did the proclamation go?
questions.a: The proclamation went throughout all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan.

questions.q: What did the proclamation say?
questions.a: The proclamation said the people should come to celebrate the Passover of Yahweh in Jerusalem.

questions.q: By what means did the proclamation go?
questions.a: The proclamation went with couriers by letters from the king and his leaders to all of Israel and Judah.

questions.q: What did the proclamation say would happen if the people turned back to Yahweh?
questions.a: The brothers and children would find compassion before those who had taken them as prisoners, and would come back into Israel.

questions.q: Where did the couriers go and how did the people respond?
questions.a: The couriers went from city to city throughout Ephraim and Manasseh all the way to Zebulun, but the people responded to them with laughing and mocking.

questions.q: Who humbled themselves and what did they do?
questions.a: Certain men of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.

questions.q: What did the hand of God do and what happened?
questions.a: The hand of God came on Judah and they had one heart to carry out the command.

questions.q: How many gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread in the second month?
questions.a: Many people, a very great assembly, gathered in Jerusalem.

questions.q: What did those gathered in Jerusalem do?
questions.a: They took away the altars, all the altars for incense, and threw them into the Kidron. Then they killed the Passover lambs on the fourteenth day of the second month.

questions.q: What did the priests and Levites who were ashamed do?
questions.a: They consecrated themselves and brought burnt offerings into the house of Yahweh.

questions.q: How did they stand and what did the priests do?
questions.a: They stood in their divisions following the law of Moses, and the priests sprinkled blood.

questions.q: Why did the priests sprinkle the blood they received from the Levites?
questions.a: Because many had not consecrated themselves, the Levites were in charge of slaughtering the Passover lambs, and the priests received it from them to sprinkle.

questions.q: Why did Hezekiah pray for the people of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, and for what did he pray?
questions.a: Many of the people had not purified themselves and ate the Passover meal against the written instructions. So Hezekiah prayed for Yahweh to pardon those who set their hearts to seek God, although they were not purified by the standards of the sanctuary.

questions.q: What did Yahweh do in response to the prayer?
questions.a: Yahweh listened to Hezekiah and healed the people.

questions.q: What did the people of Israel, the Levites, and the priests do?
questions.a: The people kept the Festival for seven days with great joy. The Levites and priests praised Yahweh singing with loud instruments.

questions.q: How did Hezekiah speak to the Levites who understood the service of Yahweh, and what did they do?
questions.a: Hezekiah encouraged them and they ate throughout the festival for seven days, offering fellowship sacrifices, and making confession to Yahweh.

questions.q: What did the whole assembly decide to do when Hezekiah gave the assembly one thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep, and the leaders gave one thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep and goats?
questions.a: The whole assembly decided to celebrate for another seven days, and they did with joy.

questions.q: Who were all those that rejoiced in the celebration?
questions.a: All the assembly of Judah, the priests, the Levites, and all the people who came together from Israel, the foreigners who came from Israel and those who lived in Judah rejoiced.

questions.q: How was the celebration described?
questions.a: There was great joy in Jerusalem, and since the time of Solomon, there had not been anything like it in Jerusalem.

questions.q: What did the priests and Levites do next in the celebration?
questions.a: They blessed the people and their voice was heard and their prayer went up to heaven.

commentary.text: Verses 1–12 Hezekiah made Israel as welcome to the passover, as any of his own subjects. Let us yield ourselves unto the Lord. Say not, you will do what you please, but resolve to do what he pleases. We perceive in the carnal mind a stiffness, an obstinacy, an unaptness to compel with God; we have it from our fathers: this must be overcome. Those who, through grace, have turned to God themselves, should do all they can to bring others to him. Numbers will be scorners, but some will be humbled and benefited; perhaps where least expected. The rich mercy of God is the great argument by which to enforce repentance; the vilest who submit and yield themselves to the Lord, seek his grace, and give themselves to his service, shall certainly be saved. Oh that messengers were sent forth to carry these glad tidings to every city and every village, through every land!

The great thing needful in attendance upon God in solemn ordinances, is, that we make heart-work of it; all is nothing without this. Where this sincerity and fixedness of heart are, there may yet be many things short of the purification of the sanctuary. These defects need pardoning, healing grace; for omissions in duty are sins, as well as omissions of duty. If God should deal with us in strict justice, even as to the very best of our doings, we should be undone. The way to obtain pardon, is to seek it of God by prayer; it must be gotten by petition through the blood of Christ. Yet every defect is sin, and needs forgiveness; and should be matter to humble, but not to discourage us, though nothing can make up for the want of a heart prepared to seek the Lord.

Many prayers were put up to God with the peace-offerings. In these Israel looked to God as the God of their fathers, a God in covenant with them. There was also abundance of good preaching. The Levites read and explained the Scriptures. Faith cometh by hearing, and true religion preaching has abounded. They sang psalms every day: praising God should be much of our work in religious assemblies. Having kept the seven days of the feast in this religious manner, they had so much comfort in it, that they kept other seven days also. This they did with gladness. Holy duties should be done with holy gladness. And when sinners humble themselves before the Lord, they may expect gladness in his ordinances. Those who taste this happiness will not soon grow weary of it, but will be glad to prolong their enjoyment.
